From: Katie Moreno <katie@nimbus-sys.com>

Date: Wed, 25 Feb 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Dedicated pool commitments — throughput & queueing specifics

Hi Jasmine,

Thanks for the demo yesterday. Nimbus is very interested in Redwood Dedicated for our inference layer, but procurement has two sticking points before we can sign:

1) We need a clear, auditable guarantee for sustained throughput per reservation (not just nominal GPU count). Our workloads are spiky but predictable; we need to avoid long tail queueing during peak minutes.
2) We need explicit behaviour for queueing/backpressure and what triggers fallback to alternate regions or model variants. If we hit reserved capacity limits, we need to know whether requests will be queued, rate-limited, or dropped and what credits (or performance credits) Redwood provides.

Can you share a short proposal that outlines minimum guaranteed throughput (for example, per-reservation concurrent request levels), tail latency targets under a 95th/99th percentile during normal and burst windows, and the escalation/credits policy? Procurement would also like a simple runbook indicating how we (Nimbus) can request carveouts or temporary burst increases.

I’ve CC'd contracts@nimbus-sys.com — they will want to review any SLA language.

Thanks,
Katie
Katie Moreno
Head of Platform Engineering, Nimbus Systems

Subject: Re: Dedicated pool commitments — throughput & queueing specifics

Hi Katie — great to hear Nimbus is close. I’ve attached a concise SLA proposal and a sample capacity plan that maps your typical daily profile to a recommended reserved pool. High level:

- Minimum reserved concurrency: we can guarantee a baseline of 40 concurrent inference requests per reserved GPU-set (this is configurable per contract).
- Tail latency SLO: 95th percentile <= 800ms for payloads up to 256 tokens under steady-state load; 99th percentile <= 1.6s. For bursts larger than configured headroom we provide graceful degradation (see next).
- Queueing & fallback: requests beyond reserved concurrency will enter a short-lived buffer (max 30s). If buffer is full we will apply adaptive shedding and route prioritized traffic according to your routing policy (region fallback or model-variant fallback).
- Bursting: customers can use a burst allowance equal to 2x baseline for up to 5 minutes. Longer bursts are subject to availability and handled via pre-agreed carveouts or on-call capacity requests.
- Credits/mitigation: if we breach guaranteed sustained throughput for reasons inside Redwood control for >6 cumulative minutes in a 24h window, we propose a credits schedule (per the attached SLA draft).

Next steps: if this aligns with procurement, I’ll loop in Ben and Laura to finalize technical wording and produce contract-ready SLA language. I’ve attached: 1) 20260225_sla_proposal_nimbus.pdf (redlined draft), 2) nimbus_capacity_plan_2026.xlsx (mapping).

Quick Q: can you share a 7-day peak-minute RPM sample so we can validate headroom assumptions?

Best,

Quick technical takes and recommended contract text below. TL;DR: numbers look reasonable with two clarifications.

1) Baseline concurrency per reserved GPU-set
- We should qualify "GPU-set" in the contract (e.g., a reserved pool of N GPUs with a target instance class). On A100-equivalent hardware we can commit to 35–45 concurrent short-form requests per GPU depending on model size. I recommend we commit to "minimum reserved concurrency of 35 concurrent inference requests per GPU" and allow customers to specify a higher guarantee at higher commit levels.

Proposed contract phrase: "Redwood will ensure a minimum reserved concurrency of 35 concurrent inference requests per reserved GPU in the customer pool for models with average context size up to 256 tokens. Customers may define a higher concurrency reservation as part of their capacity commitment."

2) Buffering/window for queueing
- 30s buffer is reasonable for short transient spikes, but to protect the pool and other tenants we should cap buffer memory per-customer. Recommend: "Requests exceeding reserved concurrency will be buffered for up to 30 seconds or until buffer capacity is exhausted; buffer capacity is defined as X MB per customer or Y concurrent buffered requests (whichever comes first)."
- To avoid exposing internal memory units in contract, propose an alternative: "buffered requests up to 30 seconds or up to 20% of the pooled buffer capacity, whichever is reached first."

3) Bursting & carveouts
- Keep the 2x 5-minute burst allowance; require 24-hour notice for planned extended bursts beyond that, or on-call approval for emergency bursts.

4) Credit/mitigation policy
- I agree the 6-minute window is a reasonable operational threshold but recommend sliding scale for credits (e.g., minor credit for 6–15 minutes, larger credit beyond 15 minutes in 24h).

Suggested addition for fallback behavior: "When reserved capacity is exhausted and buffer is full, Redwood will attempt model-variant or region fallback only if the customer's routing policy permits cross-region traffic; otherwise Redwood will apply adaptive shedding starting with unlabelled low-priority requests as defined in the customer's traffic policy."

Happy to help craft precise language. Also recommend we include an appendix with a short runbook: how to request a temporary carveout (email to <capacity-ops@redwood.com> with expected peak window, expected additional concurrency, and contact for operational approval).

Ben
